mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-01.title: Cups → ounces → pounds
mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-01.body:
Flour needed: $15 \times 2\frac14 = 33\frac34$ cups; to buy: $33\frac34 - 1 = 32\frac34$ cups.
Weight: $32.75 \times 4.8 = 157.2$ oz $= 157.2 \div 16 = 9.825$ lb. One 5-lb bag is not enough, two bags (10 lb) are.

**Answer: 2 bags**

mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-01.title: Cups per bag
mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-01.body:
A 5-pound bag is $80$ ounces, which is $80 \div 4.8 = 16\frac23$ cups. Two bags give $33\frac13$ cups $\ge 32\frac34$ cups needed, while one bag is far too little.

**Answer: 2 bags**

mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-02.title: Fraction of responses
mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-02.body:
Total responses: $63 + 18 + 18 + 9 + 27 = 135$. Cherry's share: $\frac{18}{135} = \frac{2}{15}$. Of 15 pies, that is 2 cherry pies.

**Answer: 2**

mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-02.title: Guests per pie
mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-02.body:
$135 \div 15 = 9$ guests per pie. Cherry has $18 \div 9 = 2$ pies' worth of fans.

**Answer: 2**

mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-03.title: At least 9, and even
mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-03.body:
There are $135$ guests and 15 pies, so each pie needs at least $135 \div 15 = 9$ slices. Each cut across a diameter adds 2 slices, so the number of slices is even. The smallest even number $\ge 9$ is 10.

**Answer: 10 slices**

mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-03.title: Check 8 and 10
mathcounts-potw-2026-01-26-03.body:
4 diameter cuts give 8 slices: $15 \times 8 = 120 < 135$, too few. 5 cuts give 10 slices: $150 \ge 135$ ✓.

**Answer: 10 slices**
